title: After Finishing My Clinical Clerkship at Tulane University
paragraphs: In August 2005, Hurricane Katrina, a storm of enormous force, dealt a devastating blow to a town in the southern United States. In New Orleans, a tourist city much of which lies below sea level, 80% of the inland part of the city was flooded because of the failure of the levees, and many residents died, went missing, or were forced to evacuate. Five years after that tragedy, which I had known only through the news, I stood in New Orleans and was given the chance to learn many things there over three months. It was truly fortunate for me that the exchange program with Tulane University School of Medicine was revived this academic year.

New Orleans is one of the leading tourist cities in the United States, and the university hospital is located less than a ten-minute walk from the French Quarter, a famous sightseeing spot. Thanks to a great deal of support and the desperate efforts of the residents, the center of the city has regained the relaxed atmosphere that used to be typical of the South. But if you turn into one back street, the scars of Katrina are certainly still there. At Tulane University School of Medicine too, the former veterans' hospital was left unusable but was not demolished, and the water marks on its walls from the flooding, which were painful to see, met my eyes every morning.

The first month, in cardiology, started with me feeling my way. The mornings began with a conference at 7 a.m. A theme was set for each day, and young doctors presented on it. A wide range of topics was covered in the conferences, from reading EKGs and catheterisation cases to basic medical research. After that we split into teams for rounds, but the English I had worried about did cause me trouble. At the charity hospital, many of the patients were Black people who were not very well-off. They had strong accents, and I had a great deal of trouble understanding them. In the conversations among the doctors on rounds, I could barely pick up words. In my free time I joined the scramble for the paper charts, deciphered the current problems from the hard-to-read charts, and only then did the flow of the next day's rounds begin to enter my head. At the university hospital, besides clinical care, I was allowed to observe various tests and cardiac catheterisation. Tulane University has a policy of actively performing cardiac catheterisation, and whenever I visited the cath lab there was a patient. The doctors would say, "I observed catheterisation at a hospital in Japan, and the Japanese really are better at this kind of delicate technique." Being able to hear how doctors from another country see Japanese medicine was something unique to this clerkship.

In the second month I had somehow gotten used to rounds in English. Rounds in the respiratory ICU had many young doctors such as residents, and were full of educational suggestions. The attending accurately pointed out each patient's problems and asked the doctors in charge about the treatment for each. And at every opportunity he cited trial articles from related journals. I was amazed that he remembered and presented everything, including in what year and month a trial was conducted, what its design was and what the results were. I felt that this is indeed America, the birthplace of EBM. There was also a case where the family disagreed about the future of a critically ill patient with no prospect of recovery, and I had the chance to take part in the hospital's ethics committee. I was surprised that in order to hold it, in addition to the doctors and nurses in charge, the people from the ethics department and the social workers, a medical student also had to participate. Many people put their heads together and discussed what should be done from now on and how to explain it to the family. I realised that American medicine is truly teamwork, that a great many people, including allied health professionals and others, are involved in the treatment of a single patient, and that this is why such conferences are given importance.

The third month was pediatrics, which came about because I made an unreasonable request to the person in charge there. I did my clerkship with the pediatric cardiology team, observing outpatient clinics and actually being allowed to take findings. There were also rounds in the NICU and PICU, and I was allowed to do clerkships in the pediatric ER about two days a week. I had never spoken English to children, so I struggled and often got by with facial expressions. Here I also had the opportunity to work with local students. This was one of the aims of this study abroad, and I was amazed by how highly motivated the local fourth-year students were. I also attended lectures for students, and I think they were "dynamic" lectures in which all sorts of people spoke up. I felt that the teachers here certainly have the skill to engage students and draw them out, but even more than that, the students are very good at drawing out the teacher. Whether in small-group lectures or in lectures to large numbers in a lecture hall, they ask about anything they notice or do not understand, or offer a wrong answer to the teacher's question, and when asked "Why did you think so?" they present their mistaken thinking without hesitation. And the lecture moves along at a good tempo. It was an occasion that made me reflect strongly on what attitude we students should bring to lectures in order for them to leave such a strong impression.

What I could see through the language barrier in this clinical clerkship was a "medical science" that was more similar to Japan's than I had expected, and "medical care" that was more different from Japan's than I had expected. When I saw a patient with a special bacterial infection in the ICU, the resident happened to be citing a case report from Nagoya University. Language aside, medical science is such that the results of one's own country can be applied in a country this far away. The principles of diagnosis and treatment also seem not to differ so much. I think this is because medical science is a common foundation of the world and heads toward the same goal of understanding and overcoming disease. However, the process of applying it, that is, medical care, differs greatly. The various allied health professionals, differences in the insurance system, and follow-up centred on consults: through this clerkship I experienced a great many differences.

That I was able to notice such things with my own eyes and ears was thanks to the support of really many people: the professors of the International Exchange Office, the local doctors, my fellow exchange students who encouraged each other, the seniors who came to the pre-departure training, and others. In particular, Dr. 粕谷 and 長縄さん of the International Exchange Office introduced exchange students to me from when I was a fourth-year student, and gave me the opportunity and motivation to improve my English, which I was weak in. I would like to express my heartfelt gratitude.

I think that for this study abroad program, it is not only the time spent abroad that matters. I learned a great deal in the pre-departure training, which firmly built a foothold for the start of my time abroad. And I remind myself that I must now use the experience and motivation I have brought back to Japan as a further foothold, and walk my own path in medicine steadily. The precious experience of a clinical clerkship abroad will surely continue to stimulate me, not only during the study abroad but also from before it and from now on.
Inside me, the sound of the jazz I listened to under that sultry, blazing sun still echoes.
